Dave Demers, of the NOAA Aircraft Operations Center, all commissioned officers of the NOAA Corps, flew more than 100 hours surveying Katrina’s devastation. Eastman piloted NOAA’s Bell 212 Twin Huey Helicopter from August 31 to September 19. All three men took dozens of aerial photos from an altitude of several feet to 500 feet.

quickCue: Same storm ≠ same damage：exposure + vulnerability。

name: Heat Islands
hook: Asphalt stores heat; trees provide shade.
parts: Urban heat islands are built-up areas warmer than their surroundings because hard surfaces store heat, vegetation and shade are limited, and human activities release heat.
A hot parking lot contrasts with a shaded street. More air-conditioning demand can strain the electrical grid; heat waves can worsen an existing heat island.

mnemonic.text: Heat island：asphalt 像热锅，树荫像伞。
lines: Heat island：asphalt 像热锅，树荫像伞。

fullParts: An urban heat island is an urban area that is warmer than surrounding less-developed land.
Heat-absorbing surfaces, limited vegetation and shade, and heat released by human activities increase urban temperatures.
Higher heat raises health risks and cooling demand, putting pressure on electricity systems and especially affecting vulnerable residents.
Tree cover and cooler surfaces connect urban design to environmental justice and resilience during extreme heat events.

visuals.caption: Read the temperature line: built-up areas are warmer; greener areas are cooler.

studyBlocks.text: Urban heat islands are built-up areas warmer than their surroundings because hard surfaces store heat, vegetation and shade are limited, and human activities release heat.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: A hot parking lot contrasts with a shaded street. More air-conditioning demand can strain the electrical grid; heat waves can worsen an existing heat island.

zh: 晒热的地面像锅，树荫像伞；两边站着感觉很不一样。
quickCue: Heat island：asphalt 像热锅，树荫像伞。

name: Housing Shortage/Surplus
hook: Empty luxury flats do not solve every housing shortage.
parts: A housing shortage means demand exceeds available supply; a surplus means the reverse. Housing demand is relatively inelastic because everyone needs somewhere to live.
Empty luxury flats can coexist with too few affordable homes. People may share homes, subdivide buildings or move; construction and regulation affect supply.

mnemonic.text: Musical chairs：有空房 ≠ 有住得起的房。
lines: Musical chairs：有空房 ≠ 有住得起的房。

fullParts: A housing shortage means available housing falls short of demand; a surplus means supply exceeds demand in a particular market.
Supply depends on housing units, while demand depends on population, household formation and purchasing power.
Shortages put upward pressure on rents and overcrowding; surpluses can produce vacancies even while affordable housing remains scarce.
Building regulation shapes supply, while Rosen–Roback explains how migration can adjust demand across cities.

studyBlocks.text: A housing shortage means demand exceeds available supply; a surplus means the reverse. Housing demand is relatively inelastic because everyone needs somewhere to live.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Empty luxury flats can coexist with too few affordable homes. People may share homes, subdivide buildings or move; construction and regulation affect supply.

zh: 有人找不到住得起的房子，不代表城里一间空房都没有。
quickCue: Musical chairs：有空房 ≠ 有住得起的房。

name: Filtering (Housing)
hook: Homes age; households may move up.
parts: Housing tends to filter down as it ages and loses relative quality or price, while households often move up to better housing as income rises.
Yesterday’s expensive home may become tomorrow’s starter home. Older housing can support affordability, but renovation and rising demand may reverse the process.

mnemonic.text: Filtering：houses DOWN，people UP；翻新可能反转。
lines: Filtering：houses DOWN，people UP；翻新可能反转。

fullParts: Housing filtering is the process through which older housing becomes available to lower-income households as its relative quality and price decline.
Buildings age while some households gain income and move to newer or higher-quality homes.
Older stock can provide affordable housing, although renovation, strong demand or demolition can interrupt this process.
Gentrification can reverse downward filtering by reinvesting in older neighborhoods and raising housing costs.

studyBlocks.text: Housing tends to filter down as it ages and loses relative quality or price, while households often move up to better housing as income rises.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Yesterday’s expensive home may become tomorrow’s starter home. Older housing can support affordability, but renovation and rising demand may reverse the process.

zh: 房子旧了，可能变便宜；翻新后也可能又变贵。
quickCue: Filtering：houses DOWN，people UP；翻新可能反转。

name: Building Regulation
hook: The same rulebook can protect—and exclude.
parts: Building regulation controls what, where and how people build.
Rules cover uses, lot sizes, height, parking and safety.
They can protect residents but also restrict housing supply and affordability.
Requiring large lots can exclude households unable to afford large homes.

mnemonic.text: Building rules：保护人，也可能让房更难盖。
lines: Building rules：保护人，也可能让房更难盖。

fullParts: Building regulation consists of rules governing what, where and how development can be built, including zoning and building codes.
Use restrictions, lot sizes, setbacks, height limits, parking rules and safety standards shape the amount and form of construction.
Rules can protect health and safety, but restrictive requirements can limit housing supply and exclude lower-income households.
This connects Glaeser’s builder equilibrium to Wilson’s exclusionary zoning and to NIMBY-driven housing shortages.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Building rules control uses, size, location and safety. They can protect residents, but also limit housing supply and raise costs.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A large minimum lot size can make it impossible to build smaller, cheaper homes.

zh: 盖房子的要求可以保护人，也可能让房子更难盖、更贵。
quickCue: Building rules：保护人，也可能让房更难盖。

name: Gentrification
hook: The neighborhood improves—but who can stay?
parts: Gentrification is neighborhood change caused by an inflow of wealthier residents and investment. Prices, businesses and local identity can change.

Displacement: residents leave. Gentrification-in-place: they stay but lose affordable amenities or belonging. Cultural erasure: local businesses and communities are pushed out. Displacement is possible, not inevitable.

mnemonic.text: Gentrification：富人流入 → Out / Squeezed / Erased。
lines: Gentrification：富人流入 → Out / Squeezed / Erased。

fullParts: Gentrification is neighborhood change associated with an inflow of wealthier residents and investment.
Increased demand, reinvestment and changing businesses raise housing costs and reshape local services and identity.
Existing residents may be displaced, remain under financial pressure, or experience cultural erasure even without moving.
It creates a planning dilemma: improving a neighborhood can undermine affordability, reversing filtering unless residents are protected.

studyBlocks.text: Gentrification is neighborhood change caused by an inflow of wealthier residents and investment. Prices, businesses and local identity can change.

studyBlocks.label: Three possible outcomes
studyBlocks.text: Displacement: residents leave. Gentrification-in-place: they stay but lose affordable amenities or belonging. Cultural erasure: local businesses and communities are pushed out. Displacement is possible, not inevitable.

zh: 地方变漂亮、变贵了，原来住的人可能留不下来。

visuals.caption: Old and new homes side by side: reinvestment and neighborhood change. A photo alone cannot prove displacement.

quickCue: Gentrification：富人流入 → Out / Squeezed / Erased。

name: NIMBYism
hook: “Build it—but not beside my home.”
parts: NIMBY means Not In My Back Yard: local opposition to nearby development or facilities, often over perceived neighborhood impacts.
Someone supports affordable housing but opposes it on their own street. Widespread opposition can restrict building and worsen housing shortages; concern about change can feed this resistance.

mnemonic.text: NIMBY：“支持，但别建我家旁边。”
lines: NIMBY：“支持，但别建我家旁边。”

fullParts: NIMBYism means “not in my backyard”: residents resist a proposed development or facility near them.
Concerns about traffic, neighborhood character, property values or local burdens motivate opposition.
Opposition can constrain housing supply or shift unwanted facilities elsewhere, although specific local concerns may be legitimate.
It connects to building regulation, housing shortages and participatory planning that addresses local costs alongside wider needs.

studyBlocks.text: NIMBY means Not In My Back Yard: local opposition to nearby development or facilities, often over perceived neighborhood impacts.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Someone supports affordable housing but opposes it on their own street. Widespread opposition can restrict building and worsen housing shortages; concern about change can feed this resistance.

zh: 我支持建，但别建在我家旁边。
quickCue: NIMBY：“支持，但别建我家旁边。”

name: Contact Hypothesis
hook: Liking one person may not change a prejudice.
source: Valentine: Living with Difference; Lecture 6a, slides 28–29
parts: The Contact Hypothesis says contact between different groups can reduce prejudice: knowing people may challenge assumptions about their group. Cooperation and equal standing can help.

Working with a classmate from another group may change your view. But if you think “they are nice, the rest are not,” your wider prejudice remains. That is Valentine’s critique, not the hypothesis itself.

mnemonic.text: Contact Hypothesis：多接触可能少排斥；Valentine：不保证。
lines: Contact Hypothesis：多接触可能少排斥；Valentine：不保证。

fullParts: The contact hypothesis proposes that interaction between social groups can reduce prejudice and improve relations.
Meaningful, cooperative encounters may challenge stereotypes, while competition or unequal power can obstruct that change.
Valentine shows that proximity and politeness do not necessarily change wider beliefs: a liked individual may be treated as an exception.
Mixed neighborhoods and third places therefore create opportunities for contact without automatically producing respect or inclusion.

studyBlocks.text: The Contact Hypothesis says contact between different groups can reduce prejudice: knowing people may challenge assumptions about their group. Cooperation and equal standing can help.

studyBlocks.label: Example and limit
studyBlocks.text: Working with a classmate from another group may change your view. But if you think “they are nice, the rest are not,” your wider prejudice remains. That is Valentine’s critique, not the hypothesis itself.

zh: 你喜欢一个人，不代表你就喜欢和他同一群的人。
quickCue: Contact Hypothesis：多接触可能少排斥；Valentine：不保证。

name: Sanitary Movement
hook: Make the city healthier before making it grand.
parts: The Sanitary Movement addressed disease and overcrowding in industrial cities.
Authorities improved water, sewage, waste disposal and housing conditions.
Public health became a reason for governments to plan and regulate cities.
Remember sanitation; contrast City Beautiful’s stronger focus on civic appearance.

mnemonic.text: Sanitary → sanitation：clean water IN, sewage OUT.
lines: Sanitary → sanitation：clean water IN, sewage OUT.

fullParts: The Sanitary Movement was a nineteenth-century response to disease and overcrowding in rapidly industrializing cities.
Public authorities improved water supply, sewage disposal, waste management and housing conditions to reduce health hazards.
It helped establish public health as a responsibility of urban government and a justification for planning and regulation.
It precedes City Beautiful’s emphasis on civic appearance and connects to Wilson’s concern with unequal environmental conditions.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: The Sanitary Movement made clean water, sewage, waste removal and healthier housing matters for city government.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Think “stop disease,” while City Beautiful puts more emphasis on impressive public design.

zh: 让喝的水干净，把脏水排出去，少让人生病。

visuals.caption: Clean water IN, sewage OUT. London sewer construction makes the public-health response visible.

quickCue: Sanitary → sanitation：clean water IN, sewage OUT.

name: City Beautiful
hook: Beautiful outside—but where do people live?
parts: City Beautiful, associated with Daniel Burnham in early-1900s America, used parks, boulevards and grand civic buildings to promote cleanliness, leisure and civic unity.
It expanded municipal planning power, but critics said top-down beautification neglected housing and ordinary residents. Contrast the Sanitary Movement’s health focus.

mnemonic.text: City Beautiful = 城市盛装，住房未必改善。
lines: City Beautiful = 城市盛装，住房未必改善。

fullParts: City Beautiful was an American planning movement around 1900 associated with Burnham, Robinson and Olmsted’s landscape tradition.
It used monumental civic buildings, parks and broad boulevards to promote beauty, cleanliness and civic order.
It strengthened municipal planning and created lasting public spaces, but paid less attention to housing and everyday inequalities.
Garden City pursued broader social reform, while Jacobs later criticized planning that valued visual order over street life.

visuals.caption: Grand buildings and formal public space: beauty was meant to encourage civic pride.
visuals.credit: Nichols, H. D., 1859-1939 (artist); L. Prang & Co. (publisher)

studyBlocks.text: City Beautiful, associated with Daniel Burnham in early-1900s America, used parks, boulevards and grand civic buildings to promote cleanliness, leisure and civic unity.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: It expanded municipal planning power, but critics said top-down beautification neglected housing and ordinary residents. Contrast the Sanitary Movement’s health focus.

zh: 先把城市打扮漂亮，但普通人住得好不好，可能没顾上。
quickCue: City Beautiful = 城市盛装，住房未必改善。

name: Garden City
hook: A working town inside a green belt.
parts: Ebenezer Howard wanted self-sufficient towns: people could live, work and use services locally, with countryside close by. A green belt limits outward growth, and communal land ownership serves the community.

Imagine homes, workplaces and shops inside a town surrounded by farmland and green space. It is not a bedroom suburb where everyone leaves for work. Later projects often kept the green design but weakened the social reform.

mnemonic.text: Garden City：小镇里住、工作、买东西，外面用 green belt 圈住。
lines: Garden City：小镇里住、工作、买东西，外面用 green belt 圈住。

fullParts: Ebenezer Howard’s Garden City proposed small, self-contained towns combining urban opportunities with access to countryside.
Green belts limited expansion, while communal land ownership and a balance of homes, jobs and services supported the town.
It aimed to relieve industrial overcrowding and improve living conditions; later adaptations often emphasized suburban residential design.
Unlike City Beautiful’s civic aesthetics, Garden City linked physical design to social and economic reform.

visuals.caption: THREE MAGNETS: town + country → town-country. Combine urban opportunity with rural greenery.
visuals.credit: The original uploader was Marnanel at English Wikipedia.

visuals.caption: City + green belt + planned limits. Garden City means more than adding trees.

studyBlocks.text: Ebenezer Howard wanted self-sufficient towns: people could live, work and use services locally, with countryside close by. A green belt limits outward growth, and communal land ownership serves the community.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Imagine homes, workplaces and shops inside a town surrounded by farmland and green space. It is not a bedroom suburb where everyone leaves for work. Later projects often kept the green design but weakened the social reform.

zh: 想要城里的工作和方便，也想要乡下的绿地和空间。
quickCue: Garden City：小镇里住、工作、买东西，外面用 green belt 圈住。

name: Neighborhood Unit (Clarence Perry)
hook: School in the middle, main roads at the edge.
parts: Clarence Perry’s Neighborhood Unit centers homes on a school and community facilities. Major roads bound the unit; shops sit near edge junctions, with parks and local streets inside.
It supports daily neighborhood life while discouraging through-traffic. Picture a school in the middle of a plate and main roads around its rim.

mnemonic.text: Perry：school 在盘子中间，main roads 围着盘边。
lines: Perry：school 在盘子中间，main roads 围着盘边。

fullParts: Clarence Perry’s Neighborhood Unit organizes a residential district around an elementary school and community institutions.
Major roads form its boundaries, shops sit near edge junctions, and interior streets provide local access with parks nearby.
The design aims to support neighborhood life and safer access to everyday facilities while separating through traffic.
It connects to Garden City traditions, but contrasts with Jacobs’s emphasis on continuous, interconnected mixed-use streets.

visuals.caption: School in the middle; major roads around the edge. Keep through-traffic outside.
visuals.credit: Clarence Perry / Committee on Regional Plan of New York and Its Environs

studyBlocks.text: Clarence Perry’s Neighborhood Unit centers homes on a school and community facilities. Major roads bound the unit; shops sit near edge junctions, with parks and local streets inside.

studyBlocks.label: Why this layout?
studyBlocks.text: It supports daily neighborhood life while discouraging through-traffic. Picture a school in the middle of a plate and main roads around its rim.

zh: 像一个盘子：学校放中间，大路围在边上。
quickCue: Perry：school 在盘子中间，main roads 围着盘边。

name: Modernism
hook: Sort the city into separate boxes.
parts: Modernism uses top-down, rational planning to create order and efficient transport: geometric layouts, separate functions and large planned developments.
Le Corbusier’s towers in parks illustrate this approach. Postwar urban renewal often cleared neighborhoods, bringing displacement and criticism from Jacobs.

mnemonic.text: Modernism：HOME / WORK / TRAFFIC 分开摆。
lines: Modernism：HOME / WORK / TRAFFIC 分开摆。

fullParts: Modernism in planning sought a rational, functional city through comprehensive design, geometric order and limited ornament.
Planners separated land uses and reorganized buildings, open space and movement according to standardized principles.
It promised efficiency and healthier housing, but clearance and large-scale separation could disrupt neighborhoods and everyday street life.
Jacobs challenged this approach, arguing that mixed uses and informal street activity create a complex urban order.

studyBlocks.text: Modernism uses top-down, rational planning to create order and efficient transport: geometric layouts, separate functions and large planned developments.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Le Corbusier’s towers in parks illustrate this approach. Postwar urban renewal often cleared neighborhoods, bringing displacement and criticism from Jacobs.

zh: 把住的、工作的、开车的地方分开摆，想让城市更整齐。

visuals.caption: Large blocks and open space illustrate a modernist housing form. The image alone does not explain the project’s later problems.

quickCue: Modernism：HOME / WORK / TRAFFIC 分开摆。

name: Le Corbusier/Radiant City
hook: Radiant = rise: towers in parks.
parts: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City puts tall buildings in large open spaces.
It separates activities and replaces traditional streets with planned layouts.
It promises light and efficiency but can weaken everyday street life.
Contrast Broadacre: Radiant builds upward; Broadacre spreads outward.

mnemonic.text: Radiant → RISE：高楼 + 空地。
lines: Radiant → RISE：高楼 + 空地。

fullParts: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City was a modernist vision of a highly ordered city with tall buildings surrounded by open space.
It concentrated buildings, separated functions and circulation, and moved activity away from traditional streets into planned spaces.
It promised light, air and efficiency, but related urban-renewal approaches often weakened street continuity and displaced communities.
Contrast Wright’s dispersed Broadacre City and Jacobs’s defense of mixed-use streets and informal public supervision.

visuals.caption: Brasília illustrates related modernist principles: large open spaces, separated uses and major roads. It is not Le Corbusier’s original plan.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Le Corbusier’s Radiant City puts tall buildings in open space and separates activities. It promises light and efficiency but can weaken street life.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Remember UP: towers in parks. Broadacre spreads OUT instead.

zh: 往上盖高楼，楼下留大块空地。
quickCue: Radiant → RISE：高楼 + 空地。

name: Frank Lloyd Wright/Broadacre City
hook: Broadacre = broad: spread out and drive.
parts: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Broadacre City in the 1930s proposed roughly an acre per family, dispersed development and car-based connections, integrating homes, small industry, farming and nature.
Broadacre spreads OUT; Le Corbusier’s Radiant City rises UP. Both are planned visions, but Broadacre combines work and home rather than separating every function.

mnemonic.text: BROAD-acre → OUT：摊开住，靠车走。
lines: BROAD-acre → OUT：摊开住，靠车走。

fullParts: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Broadacre City proposed a decentralized settlement pattern, with roughly an acre of land for each family.
Dispersed homes, access to nature and automobile travel replaced the compact metropolitan center.
It promised household independence and space, but required extensive land and dependence on cars.
It contrasts with Le Corbusier’s concentrated Radiant City and helps interpret auto-oriented suburban development.

visuals.caption: BROAD = spread out. Notice the large plots and road-based layout in Wright’s sketches.

studyBlocks.text: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Broadacre City in the 1930s proposed roughly an acre per family, dispersed development and car-based connections, integrating homes, small industry, farming and nature.

studyBlocks.label: Keep apart
studyBlocks.text: Broadacre spreads OUT; Le Corbusier’s Radiant City rises UP. Both are planned visions, but Broadacre combines work and home rather than separating every function.

zh: 每家摊开住，多占地，出门靠车。
quickCue: BROAD-acre → OUT：摊开住，靠车走。

name: Jane Jacobs (Death and Life of Great American Cities)
hook: Boundaries, eyes, and people throughout the day.
source: Jacobs: Uses of Sidewalks; Lecture 7a, slide 2
parts: Jane Jacobs argues that everyday street life creates order and safety.
Clear boundaries, eyes on the street and steady sidewalk use support informal supervision.
Residents, shopkeepers and passersby help watch the street.
A shopkeeper watches by day; residents watch at night. This contrasts with isolated superblocks.

mnemonic.text: Jacobs = Boundaries · Eyes · Hours.
lines: Jacobs = Boundaries · Eyes · Hours.

fullParts: In The Death and Life of Great American Cities, Jane Jacobs defended everyday street life against top-down modernist planning.
Clear public–private boundaries, eyes on the street and fairly continuous sidewalk use support informal public supervision.
Mixed uses and daily sidewalk contacts can build safety and trust without relying only on formal policing.
Her “sidewalk ballet” contrasts with superblocks and separated functions, and connects to Gehl’s and Whyte’s human-scale observations.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Jacobs says ordinary street users help keep streets safe: clear public/private boundaries, “eyes on the street,” and people using sidewalks throughout the day.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: Shopkeepers watch by day; residents and evening customers keep the street active later.

zh: 街上一直有人走、有人看，就不容易没人管。
quickCue: Jacobs = Boundaries · Eyes · Hours.

name: Urban Vitality
hook: Different reasons to visit, at different times.
parts: Urban vitality is visible street activity and the built-environment mix that sustains it. Jacobs connects varied users throughout the day to safety and everyday contact.
Density, small blocks, mixed primary uses, aged buildings, accessibility and no border vacuums. Offices bring daytime users; homes and restaurants support evening activity.

mnemonic.text: Vitality：人多 + 短街区 + 用途混 + 新旧楼 + 好到达 + 少阻隔。
lines: Vitality：人多 + 短街区 + 用途混 + 新旧楼 + 好到达 + 少阻隔。

fullParts: Urban vitality is visible street activity and the supportive built environment that sustains it.
Density, short blocks, mixed primary uses, varied building ages, accessibility and avoiding border vacuums bring different people out throughout the day.
Continuous use can support local businesses, informal supervision and sidewalk contacts, although density alone does not guarantee cohesion.
It develops Jacobs’s argument; Gehl asks whether activity includes optional and social life rather than only necessary trips.

studyBlocks.text: Urban vitality is visible street activity and the built-environment mix that sustains it. Jacobs connects varied users throughout the day to safety and everyday contact.

studyBlocks.label: Six course dimensions
studyBlocks.text: Density, small blocks, mixed primary uses, aged buildings, accessibility and no border vacuums. Offices bring daytime users; homes and restaurants support evening activity.

zh: 白天有人上班，晚上有人吃饭，街上才不容易一下空下来。
quickCue: Vitality：人多 + 短街区 + 用途混 + 新旧楼 + 好到达 + 少阻隔。

name: Transit Oriented Development
hook: Put daily life within walking distance of transit.
parts: Transit-oriented development, associated with Calthorpe, puts dense, mixed uses within walking reach of transit hubs, using connected pedestrian networks and short blocks.
Get off the train, buy groceries and walk home. Density, mixed uses and good walking connections work together; being next to tracks alone is not TOD.

mnemonic.text: TOD：train → groceries → home，全程好走。
lines: TOD：train → groceries → home，全程好走。

fullParts: Transit-oriented development concentrates dense, mixed-use, walkable development around transit stations, associated with Peter Calthorpe.
Short blocks, connected walking routes and nearby homes, shops and jobs make transit practical within roughly a ten-minute walk.
It can improve access and reduce car dependence when development and transport service work together.
TOD combines the D variables with Jacobs-style mixed use, contrasting with dispersed, auto-oriented development.

visuals.caption: Put daily destinations within walking distance of transit: station + density + mixed uses.

studyBlocks.text: Transit-oriented development, associated with Calthorpe, puts dense, mixed uses within walking reach of transit hubs, using connected pedestrian networks and short blocks.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Get off the train, buy groceries and walk home. Density, mixed uses and good walking connections work together; being next to tracks alone is not TOD.

zh: 下车、买菜、回家，都能靠走路顺手完成。
quickCue: TOD：train → groceries → home，全程好走。

name: Urban Acupuncture/Tactical Urbanism
hook: Try one useful change before a huge plan.
parts: Urban acupuncture, associated with Jaime Lerner, uses small, strategic interventions instead of one comprehensive master plan. Tactical urbanism often uses low-cost, temporary, small-scale projects.
Try temporary seating, observe use and adjust. Both connect to Lynch’s learning ecology; tactical projects can be community-led or government-led.

mnemonic.text: Acupuncture = 小针；tactical urbanism = 先便宜地试。
lines: Acupuncture = 小针；tactical urbanism = 先便宜地试。

fullParts: Urban acupuncture uses targeted interventions to improve city life; tactical urbanism often uses low-cost, temporary, small-scale projects.
Pop-up public spaces or temporary street improvements test ideas through local action rather than a complete master plan.
They can produce quick benefits and reveal how people use space, though wider problems may require lasting investment.
Lerner’s urban acupuncture connects to Lynch’s learning ecology: cities improve through adaptation and feedback.

visuals.caption: A small, inexpensive street intervention can change how a place feels and is used.

studyBlocks.text: Urban acupuncture, associated with Jaime Lerner, uses small, strategic interventions instead of one comprehensive master plan. Tactical urbanism often uses low-cost, temporary, small-scale projects.

studyBlocks.label: Example / link
studyBlocks.text: Try temporary seating, observe use and adjust. Both connect to Lynch’s learning ecology; tactical projects can be community-led or government-led.

zh: 先改一个小地方，便宜地试一下，好用再接着做。
quickCue: Acupuncture = 小针；tactical urbanism = 先便宜地试。

name: Jan Gehl (The Life Between Buildings)
hook: Good spaces make people want to stay.
parts: Jan Gehl’s Life Between Buildings links comfort, visibility, access and opportunities to linger with optional activity and low-intensity social contact.
A good bench may turn passing through into staying. Unlike Jacobs, Gehl does not require a grid or assume that greater density is always better; the experience of public space matters.

mnemonic.text: Gehl → 胶：舒服 → 留下 → 聊起来。
lines: Gehl → 胶：舒服 → 留下 → 聊起来。

fullParts: Jan Gehl’s The Life Between Buildings focuses on how public-space design supports everyday pedestrian activity and interaction.
Comfort, visibility, access and places to linger encourage optional activities alongside necessary trips, allowing social activities to result.
Better spaces support longer stays and low-intensity contacts; car-oriented spaces often reduce activity to the bare minimum.
Gehl shares Jacobs’s interest in everyday contact, but does not treat extreme density or a grid as universally desirable.

visuals.caption: Places to sit make it easier to stay. Staying creates opportunities for social activity.

studyBlocks.text: Jan Gehl’s Life Between Buildings links comfort, visibility, access and opportunities to linger with optional activity and low-intensity social contact.

studyBlocks.label: Keep apart
studyBlocks.text: A good bench may turn passing through into staying. Unlike Jacobs, Gehl does not require a grid or assume that greater density is always better; the experience of public space matters.

zh: 坐得舒服、待得开心，人才愿意留下来，才可能聊上天。
quickCue: Gehl → 胶：舒服 → 留下 → 聊起来。

name: Necessary/Resultant/Optional Activities
hook: Need → choose → interact.
parts: Gehl separates necessary, optional and resultant social activities.
Going to work is necessary; sitting in a pleasant park is optional; chatting may result.
Poor spaces mainly retain necessary activity; better spaces encourage staying.
A busy sidewalk may simply contain commuters rushing through.

mnemonic.text: Gehl：NEED 上班 → CHOOSE 坐坐 → CHAT 可能发生。
lines: Gehl：NEED 上班 → CHOOSE 坐坐 → CHAT 可能发生。

fullParts: Gehl distinguishes necessary activities, optional activities and resultant or social activities in public space.
Necessary trips must happen, such as going to work; optional activities, such as lingering, depend more on favorable conditions; social activities arise from people’s presence.
Poor spaces mainly retain necessary activity, while comfortable spaces encourage staying and opportunities for contact.
The distinction explains why pedestrian counts alone cannot establish urban vitality or the quality of social experience.

visuals.caption: Sitting outside can be OPTIONAL; conversation can emerge as a RESULTANT / social activity.

studyBlocks.label: Necessary
studyBlocks.text: Things people must do, even in poor spaces: go to work.

studyBlocks.label: Optional
studyBlocks.text: Things people choose when conditions are inviting: sit in a park.

studyBlocks.label: Resultant / social
studyBlocks.text: Activity that emerges when people are together: a conversation.

studyBlocks.label: Remember
studyBlocks.text: Better space → more staying → more chances for contact. A busy sidewalk may only mean people rushing through.

zh: 必须去上班；愿意坐一会儿；坐着坐着，可能和别人聊起来。
quickCue: Gehl：NEED 上班 → CHOOSE 坐坐 → CHAT 可能发生。

name: Kevin Lynch (Learning Ecology)
hook: Help people learn and change their city.
parts: Lynch’s learning ecology supports people in understanding, using and changing the city themselves, rather than imposing one finished master plan. Legibility and bottom-up learning matter.
Lynch’s vitality means support for basic biological needs; Jacobs’s vitality concerns lively streets. Lynch also examines sense, fit, access, control, efficiency and justice.

mnemonic.text: Lynch → LEARN：人能看懂、使用、掌控，并自己改进城市。
lines: Lynch → LEARN：人能看懂、使用、掌控，并自己改进城市。

fullParts: Kevin Lynch described the city as a learning ecology in which people adapt their surroundings and change the rules of urban life.
Good form supports vitality, sense or legibility, fit, access and control, evaluated through efficiency and justice.
People can navigate, use and improve their city rather than depend on a once-and-for-all comprehensive plan.
This supports bottom-up planning and connects to urban acupuncture, contrasting with rigid modernist order.

studyBlocks.text: Lynch’s learning ecology supports people in understanding, using and changing the city themselves, rather than imposing one finished master plan. Legibility and bottom-up learning matter.

studyBlocks.label: Keep apart
studyBlocks.text: Lynch’s vitality means support for basic biological needs; Jacobs’s vitality concerns lively streets. Lynch also examines sense, fit, access, control, efficiency and justice.

zh: 城市不是一次做完的：先试试看，再按大家用起来的情况改。
examKeywords: Lynch’s dimensions: vitality, sense, fit, access, control. Also ask about efficiency and justice.
quickCue: Lynch → LEARN：人能看懂、使用、掌控，并自己改进城市。

name: William Whyte (Social Life of Small Urban Spaces)
hook: Watch what people do, not just what designers intend.
parts: William Whyte studied how people use small public spaces.
Seating, food, street access and other people encourage staying.
Useful, welcoming spaces support informal social life.
People may sit on steps while designed seats stay empty: actual use matters.

mnemonic.text: Whyte → WHY sit HERE? 看人实际怎么用。
lines: Whyte → WHY sit HERE? 看人实际怎么用。

fullParts: William Whyte studied how people actually use small urban public spaces through systematic observation.
Comfortable seating, street connections, food and opportunities to watch others encourage people to stop and stay.
Successful spaces support informal sociability; designs that discourage unwanted users can also discourage everyone else.
His findings complement Jacobs’s street life and Gehl’s optional activities, while triangulation explains how shared attractions prompt conversation.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Whyte watched what people actually do in public spaces. Places to sit, food, street access and other people help attract users.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: People crowd onto steps while formal seats stay empty. Observe use instead of trusting the design on paper.

zh: 别只看设计图好不好看，看看人到底愿意坐在哪里。

visuals.caption: Seats, trees and water. Ask Whyte’s question: where do people actually choose to stay?

quickCue: Whyte → WHY sit HERE? 看人实际怎么用。

name: Triangulation
hook: Two strangers + a third thing = a conversation.
parts: Whyte’s triangulation happens when a shared attraction prompts strangers to interact.
Art, a performer or an unusual event gives them a common topic.
People who would otherwise stay separate may start talking.
Two strangers commenting on the same street performance form the triangle.

mnemonic.text: Triangulation：两个人 + 一个共同关注的东西。
lines: Triangulation：两个人 + 一个共同关注的东西。

fullParts: Whyte’s triangulation occurs when a shared external stimulus gives strangers a reason to interact.
An artwork, performance or unusual event attracts their attention and provides a common topic.
People who would otherwise remain separate may exchange comments and briefly form a social connection.
It links public-space design to Gehl’s resultant activities, but Valentine reminds us that a brief encounter does not guarantee lasting respect.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Triangulation happens when a shared attraction gives strangers a reason to talk.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You and a stranger comment on the same street performer: person → performer ← person.

zh: 两个不认识的人，因为都在看同一个表演，就有话说了。

visuals.caption: A performer gives strangers a shared focus that can start a conversation.

quickCue: Triangulation：两个人 + 一个共同关注的东西。

name: Ray Oldenburg (Third Places)
hook: Home first, work second, familiar hangout third.
parts: Oldenburg’s third places host regular, informal gatherings outside home and work.
They offer neutrality, equality, conversation, access, regulars, simplicity, playfulness and belonging.
Repeated meetings help build community ties.
Think of a familiar café; regulars and atmosphere matter more than attracting the biggest crowd.

mnemonic.text: Third place：1 home · 2 work · 3 hangout。
lines: Third place：1 home · 2 work · 3 hangout。

fullParts: Ray Oldenburg’s third places are informal gathering places outside home and work that sustain regular social life.
They offer neutral ground, social leveling, conversation, accessibility, regulars, a low profile, playfulness and a sense of being at home.
Repeated voluntary encounters create belonging and everyday community ties.
Unlike approaches emphasizing foot traffic alone, Oldenburg stresses social character and regulars; this connects to Putnam’s concern about social capital.

visuals.caption: A familiar café can be a THIRD place: neither home nor work, but somewhere to meet regularly.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Oldenburg’s third places are informal gathering spots beyond home and work, where regulars meet and conversation feels easy.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: A familiar café where you can linger and chat. Community comes from repeated contact, not just a big crowd.

zh: 家以外、工作以外，有个常去坐坐、和熟人聊聊的地方。
examKeywords: Eight traits: neutral ground, equality, conversation, accessibility, regulars, low profile, playful mood, a home away from home.
quickCue: Third place：1 home · 2 work · 3 hangout。

name: Georg Simmel (“Blasé Man”/”Protective Organ”)
hook: The city is loud; the mind turns down the volume.
parts: Simmel argues that constant urban stimulation can lead people to reduce their emotional reactions. The blasé attitude acts as a protective organ: a mental defense against overload, not a literal body part.

After passing noise, advertisements and crowds all day, you stop reacting strongly to each one. This is an internal response; Goffman’s civil inattention is an outward ritual of giving strangers privacy.

mnemonic.text: Simmel：声音、人、事情太多，给自己的反应“调低音量”。
lines: Simmel：声音、人、事情太多，给自己的反应“调低音量”。

fullParts: Georg Simmel’s blasé attitude describes emotional reserve developed in response to the intense stimulation of metropolitan life.
Individuals filter the constant flow of encounters and impressions, creating a psychological “protective organ.”
This helps people cope but can make urban relations seem impersonal or indifferent.
Unlike Goffman’s civil inattention, which concerns interaction rituals, Simmel emphasizes the mental response to urban overstimulation.

studyBlocks.text: Simmel argues that constant urban stimulation can lead people to reduce their emotional reactions. The blasé attitude acts as a protective organ: a mental defense against overload, not a literal body part.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: After passing noise, advertisements and crowds all day, you stop reacting strongly to each one. This is an internal response; Goffman’s civil inattention is an outward ritual of giving strangers privacy.

zh: 城里声音和人太多，只好让自己别对每件事都有强烈反应。
quickCue: Simmel：声音、人、事情太多，给自己的反应“调低音量”。

name: Louis Wirth (“Collective Personality”)
hook: Size + density + diversity change social life.
parts: Wirth links large population size, density and heterogeneity to a shared urban pattern of behavior: people often relate through specialized roles rather than knowing one another personally. This is a collective personality, not everyone having an identical personality.

You know the cashier as the person who takes payment, not their family or life story. Wirth explains social relationships under urban conditions; Simmel focuses on mental protection against stimulation.

mnemonic.text: Wirth：人多又不同，认得“做什么”，不一定熟悉“这个人”。
lines: Wirth：人多又不同，认得“做什么”，不一定熟悉“这个人”。

fullParts: Louis Wirth argued that urbanism is a way of life shaped by large population size, density and social heterogeneity.
These conditions encourage specialized roles and more impersonal, segmented relationships among people who cannot know everyone personally.
Urban residents develop shared patterns of behavior, described in class as a collective personality, to navigate city life.
Contrast Jacobs, who emphasizes how these same conditions can support vitality, neighborhood contact and social cohesion.

studyBlocks.text: Wirth links large population size, density and heterogeneity to a shared urban pattern of behavior: people often relate through specialized roles rather than knowing one another personally. This is a collective personality, not everyone having an identical personality.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: You know the cashier as the person who takes payment, not their family or life story. Wirth explains social relationships under urban conditions; Simmel focuses on mental protection against stimulation.

zh: 人多又各不相同，不可能个个熟悉，常常只认识对方做什么工作。
quickCue: Wirth：人多又不同，认得“做什么”，不一定熟悉“这个人”。

name: Erving Goffman (“Civil Inattention”)
hook: “I see you, but I will not bother you.”
parts: Goffman’s civil inattention is polite attention management among strangers.
A brief glance or nod is followed by looking away.
People acknowledge each other while protecting privacy.
Not staring at someone in an elevator is a social courtesy, not necessarily coldness.

mnemonic.text: Goffman → gaze OFF：看一眼，再移开目光。
lines: Goffman → gaze OFF：看一眼，再移开目光。

fullParts: Erving Goffman’s civil inattention is the polite management of attention among strangers sharing public space.
A brief glance, nod or small avoidance gesture acknowledges another person without inviting unwanted involvement.
These rituals preserve privacy and allow people to coexist comfortably in crowded settings.
Unlike Simmel’s psychological defense against overstimulation, civil inattention is an interaction practice; apparent ignoring can be social courtesy rather than hostility.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Civil inattention means briefly acknowledging a stranger, then looking away to give them privacy.

studyBlocks.label: Picture it
studyBlocks.text: In an elevator, a quick glance followed by looking away is polite—not necessarily unfriendly.

zh: 看一眼，知道你在，然后移开目光，不一直盯着你。
quickCue: Goffman → gaze OFF：看一眼，再移开目光。

name: “Bowling Alone” (Robert Putnam)
hook: One bowler where a league used to gather.
parts: Putnam’s Bowling Alone argues that civic participation and social capital have declined.
Less involvement can weaken networks, trust and cooperation.
Communities may find collective action harder.
Aelbrecht adds that social life may move to newer places, such as malls, rather than simply disappear.

mnemonic.text: Bowling Alone：球还在打，固定一起打的人少了。
lines: Bowling Alone：球还在打，固定一起打的人少了。

fullParts: Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone argues that social capital and community participation have declined in the United States.
Reduced involvement in associations and more solitary activity weaken networks, trust and habits of cooperation.
This can reduce the ties that support collective action and everyday community life.
Oldenburg emphasizes gathering places, while Aelbrecht qualifies Putnam’s account: interaction may shift from traditional organizations to newer spaces such as malls.

studyBlocks.label: In plain English
studyBlocks.text: Putnam argues that declining civic participation weakens social capital: networks, trust and cooperation.

name: Dexter. Transportation and Land Use.
hook: Land use ↔ transport.
parts: Land use and transportation shape each other.
Development creates travel needs, while networks change accessibility and the attractiveness of locations.
Use Dexter to explain suburbanization, land values and why wider roads can induce additional driving.
Connect the land–travel trade-off to AMM and compare road expansion with TOD.

name: Glaeser. The Economics Approach to Cities (Excerpt).
hook: Good locations bring benefits—and offsetting costs.
source: Glaeser. The Economics Approach to Cities (Excerpt).
parts: Glaeser uses spatial equilibrium to explain the choices of workers, firms and builders.
Workers balance income and amenities against housing and travel costs; firms need productivity to justify high costs.
Use this framework to explain why high wages or attractive amenities can come with high rents.
Distinguish AMM within cities from Rosen–Roback across cities; judge policy by its effects on people.

name: Boeing. Off the Grid… and Back Again?
hook: A grid needs three features together.
source: Boeing. Off the Grid… and Back Again?
parts: Boeing measures street-network griddedness through orientation order, straightness and four-way intersections.
US networks moved away from grids and later partly returned; more grid-like areas are associated with lower car ownership.
Use the study to discuss the long-lasting effects of street design and connectivity.
Connect to the D variables and Jacobs’s small blocks, without turning association into a causal claim.

name: Galster et al. Wrestling Sprawl to the Ground.
hook: Sprawl is a pattern with eight dimensions.
source: Galster et al. Wrestling Sprawl to the Ground.
parts: Galster separates urban development patterns from their causes and consequences.
The eight dimensions are density, continuity, concentration, clustering, centrality, nuclearity, mixed uses and proximity.
Use these dimensions to explain how two places with similar density can have very different forms.
Connect to Boeing’s street networks; avoid treating every undesirable urban outcome as a definition of sprawl.

name: Wilson et al. How Planning and Zoning Contribute to Inequitable Development, Neighborhood Health, and Environmental Justice
hook: Planning distributes healthy environments unequally.
source: Wilson et al. How Planning and Zoning Contribute to Inequitable Development, Neighborhood Health, and Environmental Justice
parts: Wilson and colleagues connect planning and zoning to unequal neighborhood health and environmental justice.
Exclusionary zoning and fragmented local governance can concentrate hazards while limiting access to healthier surroundings.
Use riskscapes to connect housing, transport, pollution, food access and physical activity.
Neighborhood improvement should benefit existing residents; connect this to gentrification and displacement.

name: Jedwab and Vollrath. Urbanization Without Growth in Historical Perspective.
hook: Urbanization does not automatically mean development.
source: Jedwab and Vollrath. Urbanization Without Growth in Historical Perspective.
parts: Jedwab and Vollrath show that the relationship between urbanization and income changes historically.
Countries can now have higher urban shares at comparable income levels; urbanization is not simply industrial growth.
Use rural push, urban bias, improved urban survival and natural population increase to explain the gap.
Connect resource-financed consumption cities to the difference between urban population growth and productivity growth.

name: Ihlanfeldt. The Spatial Mismatch Between Jobs and Residential Locations in Urban Areas.
hook: Suburban jobs + residential barriers = spatial mismatch.
source: Ihlanfeldt. The Spatial Mismatch Between Jobs and Residential Locations in Urban Areas.
parts: Ihlanfeldt examines the separation of disadvantaged workers from suitable employment.
Residential segregation, job decentralization, transport barriers, hiring and information problems can limit employment opportunities.
Use this to explain why jobs existing somewhere in a region does not mean everyone can access them.
Compare moving people to jobs, jobs to people, or improving connections; contrast Grengs’s emphasis on mode.

name: Grengs. Job Accessibility and the Modal Mismatch in Detroit.
hook: A good location by car can be a poor location by transit.
source: Grengs. Job Accessibility and the Modal Mismatch in Detroit.
parts: Grengs argues that Detroit’s job-access problem cannot be understood from residential location alone.
Car access can be relatively strong where transit access is weak, and competition for jobs also matters.
Use modal mismatch to explain why neighborhood averages can hide disadvantages for residents without cars.
Connect to Ihlanfeldt, distinguish accessibility from mobility, and consider trips involving work, childcare and shopping.

name: Jacobs. The Death and Life of Great American Cities (Excerpt).
hook: Busy sidewalks can provide informal supervision.
source: Jacobs. The Death and Life of Great American Cities (Excerpt).
parts: Jacobs argues that everyday street users help maintain safety through informal public supervision.
Clear public–private boundaries, eyes on the street and fairly continuous sidewalk use support this order.
Use mixed uses and shops to explain why people arrive at different times and have reasons to watch.
Contrast modernist separation and quiet superblocks; connect to Gehl and Whyte without assuming density alone ensures safety.

mnemonic.text: Jacobs → 街口：有人看 + 一直有人用 → safety。

name: Valentine. Living with Difference.
hook: Sharing space is not the same as respecting difference.
parts: Valentine questions the assumption that everyday encounters automatically create respect between groups.
Proximity can lack interaction, politeness can coexist with prejudice, and liked individuals may be treated as exceptions.
Use the reading to qualify claims that mixed neighborhoods or lively public spaces necessarily produce inclusion.
Connect the contact hypothesis to unequal power and meaningful interaction; distinguish tolerance from changed group attitudes.

name: Borer. Being in the City.
hook: People sense cities—and learn what those sensations mean.
parts: Borer examines urban experience through sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
Sensory meanings are socially learned through shared practices rather than being purely individual reactions.
Use locational socialization to explain how activities and sensory experiences create shared meanings of place.
Connect to Simmel’s overstimulation and Goffman’s interaction rituals; distinguish urbanism as lived experience from urbanization as growth.

name: Video: William Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
hook: Sitting, street connection, sun, water, trees and food.
source: Video: William Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
parts: Whyte’s film asks why some public spaces attract people while others remain underused.
Observations show the importance of seating choices, street access, food and people-watching; people often choose edges rather than empty centers.
Use movable chairs or street-connected plazas as concrete evidence that everyday behavior matters more than a plan’s appearance.
Connect to Gehl’s optional activities and Jacobs’s street life; exclusionary design can drive away ordinary users too.
